text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Russian newspapers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
KOMMERSANT DAILY

- Figures in a declaration on personal wealth submitted by entrepreneur Boris Berezovsky, now a deputy secretary of the Kremlin Security Council, differ from an estimate of his fortune by the U.S. magazine Forbes.
- A conflict between central bank chairman Sergei Dubinin and former deputy finance minister Andrei Vavilov has entered a new stage with Vavilov's allegations of impropriety against the banker.
- Top managers of state-controlled Moscow Narodny Bank in London bow out after a major shake-up.
- Russian carrier Aeroflot continues its rock-bottom fare policies in what it considers to be a successful attempt to lure more customers to its flights.
- Russia has already sent managers to study abroad twice in recent times.
- A conflict between shareholders of Moscow relay broadcaster Kosmos-TV and its former managing director continues unabated.
- The U.S. Energy Secretary on a visit to Moscow has urged his Russian counterpart to open up the domestic nuclear energy market.
- The government has ruled to break natural gas giant Gazprom's monopoly on using Russia's gas pipelines.
- President Yeltsin has given the go-ahead to an issue of convertible bonds by Unified Energy Systems.
- President Boris Yeltsin has stopped short of signing a decree liberalising gold exports.
- Gazprom seems to be ready to go out of its way to make its debtors pay.
SEVODNYA
- President Yeltsin, spending much of his time working during his holiday break in Central Russia, seems to be experiencing a 'second youth'.
- Russia and the U.S. are to introduce stricter controls over use of nuclear energy.
- The central bank has reshuffled top management at the Moscow Narodny Bank in London.
- Russian steel producers refuse to accept U.S. trade ministry accusations they export steel at dumping prices.
- The Moscow regional administration has conceded it has lost control over Unikombank.
- Japanese automaker Toyota has confirmed its plans to open an assembly line for commercial vehicles in Moscow.
NEZAVISIMAYA GAZETA

- President Boris Yeltsin should have turned down the law on religious organisations in Russia before a stream of petitions from foreign officials urging him to do so spilled onto newspaper front pages.
- Russia's financial system will not be able to develop properly if the central bank is used by politicians in their power games.
- President Yeltsin has expressed satisfaction with the way the Russian gold market is developing.
- Russian telecommunications giant Svyazinvest is likely to be auctioned off at prices well below its real value.
- President Yeltsin has virtually stripped the Yakut diamond-mining company Alrosa of the right to sell diamonds at market prices.
- Foreign investors ask the President and the government to make clear the real value of shares in Russia's giant Norilsk Nickel smelter.
IZVESTIA

- A decision by Russia's Gazprom natural gas monopoly to cut the amount of gas delivered to debt-ridden Belarus and Ukraine shows that the company may be moving away from political considerations in its business strategy.
- Russia's Atomic Energy ministry considers boosting uranium sales a top priority while its U.S. counterpart is more concerned about strict controls over such exports.
- President Yeltsin has reserved for himself the ultimate right to decide who among the many refugees coming to Russia should be granted political immigrant status.

- Alexander Pochinok, head of the tax service and shareholder in Mechel metals smelter, has promised tough measures against the company, as well as a number of other tax-dodgers, if they do not pay all their debts to the budget.
- The first Hi-Ace commercial vehicles the Japaneese automaker Toyota is planning to assemble in Russia could leave the factory as early as 1999.
- Russia urgently needs a law on prevention of mafia infiltration into the banking system.
ROSSIISKIYE VESTI
- The idea to send Russian state officers abroad for training will yield fruit only if those chosen for the scheme are truly bright and talented.

- Coordinated work by the executive branch of power and the legislators should make it possible to quickly overcome the many shortcomings of the law on religious organisations in Russia which prompted President Yeltsin to turn it down.
- President Yeltsin's choice of the Northern Russian republic of Karelia as his holiday destination could give a boost to the tourist sector of the region's crisis-stricken economy.

- The Russian Orthodox Church has urged President Yeltsin to be swift in signing the law on religious organisations in Russia but the sphere of confessional freedom is exactly that part of public life where one has to think twice before making a decision.
MOSKOVSKY KOMSOMOLETS
- A shot fired at the apartment of Central Bank chairman Sergei Dubinin could mark an intensification of turf battles in Russia's banking sector.
- A tax of about $10 will be levied on everyone crossing the Russian border.
--Andrei Shukshin, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
